newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu and Arafat may hold summit - officials.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu and Arafat may hold summit - officials.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, pressed to move swiftly to rescue a crippled peace process, may meet Palestinian President Yasser Arafat next week, Israeli and Palestinian officials said on Sunday.
Officials earlier said formal Israeli-Palestinian talks on a long-delayed troop redeployment from the West Bank town of Hebron, set to reconvene on Monday, will be postponed for at least one day.
One Palestinian official, who spoke on condition he not be identified, said a Netanyahu-Arafat meeting could take place on Wednesday.
"There are signs of such a meeting, I cannot deny this," Netanyahu aide David Bar-Illan said, adding that he could not discuss details.
Palestinian sources said U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross discussed the possible summit with Arafat at a meeting late on Sunday in the West Bank town of Nablus.

Netanyahu resisted meeting Arafat after the hardline Israeli leader took office in June, but reluctantly agreed to meet him in September after Israeli President Ezer Weizman said he would hold talks with Arafat should Netanyahu continue to refuse.
Arafat and Netanyahu met again early this month at an emergency summit in Washington after fierce Palestinian-Israeli clashes last month in which 60 Arabs and 15 Jews were killed.
The fighting threatened to scuttle the 1993 Israel-PLO peace deal, and sparked fears of a return to Arab-Israeli warfare.

Earlier on Sunday Ross, referring to informal Israeli-PLO contacts, said he proposed a one-day delay "to give the ongoing discussions an opportunity to develop further and create a stronger basis for making progress when the talks convene."
Officials said the delay in the talks due to be held at Egypt's Red Sea resort of Taba could be longer than one day.
Ross, mediator in formal talks launched last week, said recent meetings between the two sides had proved "very useful."
Israeli and Palestinian officials confirmed that they had agreed to the delay, but they differed sharply on the extent to which any progress had been made.
Senior Israeli negotiator Dan Shomron said the informal negotiations had spurred a narrowing of gaps between the sides. "It would be a shame to halt the momentum," he told army radio.

Palestinian negotiator Hassan Asfour rejected Israeli reports of progress. "Contrary to what is being reported on progress, differences still exist. There is a wide gap between the two sides," Asfour told Reuters.
Another Palestinian negotiator, Saeb Erakat, said talks with Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu's government had failed to yield "one inch of progress."
Erekat called on Washington, Israel's main ally, to push the Jewish state to honour a Hebron pullout deal signed with the Labour government ousted by Netanyahu in May elections.
The Hebron redeployment is seen as an acid test of Netanyahu's intentions towards the Middle East peace process.
The latest talks were an outgrowth of the Washington summit.
Formal negotiating sessions were held in Israeli and Palestinian-controlled areas of the Gaza Strip last week and officials said informal talks had since continued.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat pointedly hosted Israeli opposition leader Shimon Peres on Sunday in self-ruled Nablus, the only West Bank town still under an Israeli blockade imposed after last month's violence.
